title: The Seven Hunters
summary: On the Flannan Isles, the light went dark on 15 December 1900, and when the relief boat finally reached the rock eleven days later, its three keepers were gone. The station was found closed and tidy: the lamp trimmed for evening, the clock stopped, one coat still on its peg. Room by room, the island gives up what happened in daylight on the 15th: a gale, a box of ropes at the west landing that one man could not afford to lose, and a sea that came up the cliff higher than anyone thought a sea could.

characters.name: Joseph Moore

art.description: wiry relief lighthouse keeper in his thirties, soaked navy double-breasted Northern Lighthouse Board jacket with brass buttons, peaked cap with brass badge, pale drawn face, one hand gripping an iron pole
idle: gripping the iron pole, staring up the cliff steps
glancing back over his shoulder toward the sea
wiping rain from his face with his free hand

dialogue: No flag. No boxes. Not a soul at the rail. You'll have seen it from the deck, miss.
The light's been dark since the fifteenth. We lay stormbound six days, the whole crew of us watching west for it.
I went up alone. Gate shut. Door shut. Fire dead in the range, the clock stopped, the beds made. Nobody.
I shouted every name I had. The house just sat there and let me.
I came out and I locked the door behind me. Don't ask me why. I didn't want anything following me down.
Here. The station key. If you're set on going up, you'll go with that, for I'll not. Not till the mate's ready.
And miss. There's an old man standing in the chapel ruin, east of the yard. I saw him plain.
There's been no old man on this rock since they built the light.
afterwards: I'll go back up when the mate's ready, and not before.
The chapel's east of the yard, through the gap in the wall. Don't stop long in that yard.

The keepers ran up the flag whenever the tender came in sight, so the Hesperus would know all was well. On the 26th she looked for it and saw an empty pole.
The halyard is neatly made fast to its cleat and coiled the Board way. Someone put it away properly, and no one has touched it since.

examine: An empty iron tramway truck at the head of the incline, its wheel chocked with a wedge of wood driven hard home.
A painted notice on the post beside it: 'KEEPERS WILL SECURE THE TRUCK BEFORE ANY GALE. BY ORDER.'
They did. Whatever happened on the 15th, they had time to see to the truck, and they did it carefully, the way they did everything.
afterwards: The chock holds. The truck hasn't moved an inch in eleven days.

props.name: black iron gatepost hung with a heavy wet chain and a brass Board padlock
examine: The west gate. A Board padlock and a length of chain hold it shut against the wind, and the painted board above it reads WEST LANDING.
Beyond the bars, a path drops away toward the far side of the island. Somewhere down there the sea is booming, louder than it should be.
By standing order the principal keeper carries the key to this gate on him. Wherever Mr Ducat is, the key is with him.
afterwards: The padlock is cold and wet and will not give. Mr Ducat has the key.

examine: A flat slab, worn smooth and faintly hollowed by centuries of hands.
Above it, in the little niche in the north wall, lies a small iron key on a split ring, laid square, the way someone lays an offering.
The paper tag is damp but legible, in a careful hand: 'Oil Store, T.M.'
afterwards: The niche is empty now. The altar stone waits, as patient as it has always been.

The fowlers stopped here first, before any work on the island: heads uncovered, a turn sunwise round the cell, a prayer at this door.

The Lewis men who slept here came out for the seabirds' eggs and the sheep, and only in fair summer weather.
No one ever stayed on this island through a winter. Not until the light was built.

characters.name: Old Murdo the Fowler

art.description: gaunt old Hebridean fowler ghost from an earlier century, bareheaded, knitted bonnet clutched in both hands, homespun plaid belted over coarse shirt, bare feet, coil of horsehair rope over one shoulder, drained grey and faintly see-through
idle: standing bareheaded, head bowed, bonnet held in both hands
lifting his head slightly to look at the viewer, bonnet still in his hands

dialogue: Bonnet off on this ground, lass. Though you've none to take off.
We came out in the long days for the birds and the sheep. First thing off the boat: heads bare, a turn sunwise round the cell, and a prayer at this door.
And no common names. We never called it the sea here. We called it the Great Grey. The island listens, and it is better it hears nothing it knows.
Eleven days gone, in broad day and a howling gale, a young keeper ran past my wall. Oilskin on him, running west for the far landing.
Something fell from his belt and he never turned for it. A man running like that is not thinking of what he drops.
I picked it up and laid it on the altar stone, in the little niche in the north wall of my chapel.
It's a key with a tag on it. Take it. I've no doors to open.
Mind how you go west. The Great Grey has men of its own, and in a storm they come up to fetch more.
afterwards: The niche, lass. Above the altar stone, in the north wall.
Go sunwise, and keep your names to yourself.

rooms.name: The Kitchen Where the Clock Stopped
rooms.walls: varnished pine matchboard panelling above a whitewashed plaster dado, smoke-darkened near the ceiling

doors.art: The main station door in the north face of the keepers' block, painted Board buff with a brass knob, a brass letter plate and a small pane of glass faintly amber from the lantern inside. Moore locked it when he fled.
A plain four-panel pine door in the kitchen's west wall, standing ajar

props.name: cold black cast-iron kitchen range, oven doors shut, grate full of fine grey ash, cold iron kettle on the hotplate, brass rail, front view
examine: The range is stone cold. The fire went out on its own and burned down to fine grey ash.
It wasn't raked or banked. It just died, days ago.
Coal is still laid ready in the scuttle beside it. No one came back to use it.
afterwards: Cold ash. Days old.

props.name: plain round Northern Lighthouse Board wall clock with brass bezel and still pendulum in a pine case, hands stopped
examine: The pendulum hangs dead still.
A keeper winds this clock every morning without thinking about it, the way he washes his face.
If no one wound it, no one was here to wind it.
afterwards: The hands haven't moved.

props.name: pine board with three iron coat pegs, one long ochre oilskin coat and sou'wester hanging from it, the other two pegs empty
examine: Three pegs. One coat.
The collar is inked in a careful hand: 'D. MacA.'
Two men put on their oilskins before going out into a gale.
The third went out in his shirtsleeves and never stopped for his coat.
afterwards: One coat, still damp at the hem. 'D. MacA.'

examine: The table is scrubbed white. Plates washed and racked, pots hung, the floor swept.
No half-eaten meal, whatever the stories will later say.
This was a tidy house, left in an ordinary moment.
The only thing out of place is the chair by the door, and Moore knocked that over himself, running out.
afterwards: Clean. Ordinary. Empty.

The Weather Slate

parts.art: wooden-framed school slate hung on a nail, chalked in a careful hand with columns of dates, wind, sea and barometer readings, the bottom rows blank

examine: Columns in neat chalk: wind, sea, barometer. 13th December. 14th December. Gale noted, sea high.
15th December, morning: wind W, strong gale. Barometer falling. Then the rows below are clean slate.
The noon entry was never written. Nor the evening one.
It was waiting to be copied into the book tonight, the way it was every night. Someone was meant to come back and do it.
afterwards: The chalk stops on the morning of the 15th. Below it, the slate is blank.

props.name: principal keeper's sloped pine writing desk with a leather logbook lying open on the lid, inkwell and pen beside it, front view
examine: The station logbook lies open, the pen laid square beside it. Principal Keeper Ducat's hand: small, upright, dutiful.
Weather. Oil used. Lamp lit at such an hour, extinguished at such an hour. Stores received. Nothing else, ever.
The ink entries stop a day or more before the slate does. He wrote it up in batches, when there was time.
There is not one strange word on any page. Whatever happened came all at once, to men who meant to sit here tonight and write it down.
afterwards: Neat, dull entries, and then blank paper. He expected to finish them this evening.

props.name: plain wooden kitchen chair pushed slightly askew, front view
The Duty Roster

parts.art: framed handwritten Northern Lighthouse Board duty roster under glass, one name struck through in ink with another written beside it

examine: NORTHERN LIGHTHOUSE BOARD. FLANNAN ISLANDS STATION.
Principal Keeper: J. Ducat. Assistant Keeper: T. Marshall.
Assistant Keeper: W. Ross. Struck through in ink, and beside it, 'sick leave'.
Written in under it, in a different hand: 'D. MacArthur, occasional keeper.'
MacArthur was never meant to be on this rock this winter. He was only standing in.
afterwards: Ross, sick leave. MacArthur written in beside him, standing in.

props.name: The Key Board

parts.art: varnished pine key board with two rows of brass hooks, small iron keys hanging on most, paper tags under each hook, two hooks empty

examine: A varnished board of brass hooks, every one with a paper tag in a careful hand. Coal house. Boat shed. Fog signal.
One empty hook. Its tag reads 'Oil Store, T.M.' Marshall's initials. He took the store key with him when he went.
A second empty hook: 'West Gate'. Beneath it, a pinned slip: 'By standing order, to be carried by the Principal Keeper.'
So Ducat has the west gate key on him, wherever he is. And Moore said there was someone standing in the chapel ruin, east of the yard.
afterwards: Two empty hooks: 'Oil Store, T.M.' and 'West Gate', the principal keeper's to carry.

In a bad sea that box was the first thing at risk. Whoever kept this rack counted it often.

examine: The oil for the light, racked and measured. Each cask has a level mark chalked on its head, with a tally beside it.
The last tally reads the 15th of December: oil drawn and carried up to the lamp, the same as any other day.
Whatever took the keepers away, it didn't stop the morning's work.
afterwards: The last tally is the 15th: oil carried up, as on any day.

props.name: Northern Lighthouse Board printed notice with a red wax seal, soft and creased from folding, pinned up by a nail
examine: A Board notice, nailed up hard by the door where a man would see it every time he came in.
'Assistant Keeper T. Marshall is hereby fined five shillings for landing gear lost at the West Landing during a gale.'
'Keepers are reminded that all equipment must be properly secured.'
The paper has been folded and unfolded so many times it has gone soft as cloth.
afterwards: Fined five shillings for gear lost at the West Landing. The paper has gone soft from handling.

characters.name: Thomas Marshall

art.description: ghost of a young assistant lighthouse keeper with a pale fresh face, ochre oilskin coat and sou'wester pouring seawater, sea boots, holding a coil of tarred rope in both hands, drained of colour, grey and dripping
idle: head down, turning the rope coil in his hands, counting
lifting the coil slightly, lips moving as he counts
turning the coil the other way, water running off his hat brim
glancing up anxiously toward the door

dialogue: Twenty-two coils. Twenty-two. And the handles, all labelled. That's the spares. The spares are all right.
It's the box at the west landing I'm feared for. Crane handles, ropes, the lot, wedged up in the rock a hundred and ten feet above the water. And still the gale gets at it.
They docked my pay the last time the gale took the gear. Five shillings, and a notice from the Board. I'll not be docked twice.
On the fifteenth it was blowing something terrible. Mr Ducat said we'd get our oilskins on, go down together and lash it, and be back for the lamp.
Donald was to bide by the fire. He's only the occasional man, standing in for Ross. No sense three of us getting soaked.
I don't remember coming back up. That's daft. I must have. I'm here, amn't I?
Funny. I can still hear the sea in my ears, and I've been out of it for days.
Here. Mr Ducat's up the tower. Take him this, he'll want it before dark. The lamp door's at the back of the kitchen, the north wall.
afterwards: Twenty-two coils... Go on, miss. Mr Ducat's waiting on that key.
The lamp door. Back of the kitchen, north wall. Before dark, mind.

props.name: great prismatic lighthouse lens, a tall beehive of glass prisms in a polished brass frame with an unlit brass oil lamp and spotless glass chimney visible inside, front view
props.material: polished brass
examine: The great lens: a beehive of glass prisms in a brass cage, taller than a man.
Not a smear on it, not a fleck of salt. It was cleaned by hand, slowly, the way a careful keeper cleans it every day.
Inside, the lamp waits. The wick is cut level, the chimney spotless, the burner ready.
Everything was done for the evening's lighting, and it was never struck.
afterwards: The prisms hold the last of the dusk like water. The wick is still cut level, waiting.

props.name: brass wall shelf holding a row of full brass oil fountains and paraffin canteens, front view
examine: Brass oil fountains and canteens, every one full to the brim.
Enough paraffin for the whole night. Men who meant to be away would not have filled them.
Whatever happened, it happened in daylight, with the day's work done.
afterwards: Full to the brim. They meant to be back before dark.

props.name: tall narrow deep-set tower window with iron glazing bars showing a violet dusk sky over a grey island and dark sea
examine: From up here the whole island lies below, grey under the dusk.
To the west, a narrow cleft in the cliff where a crane stands: the west landing.
The turf at the top of the cleft looks torn away, as if something enormous came up it.
afterwards: The west landing. The torn turf shows raw and brown even from here.

characters.name: James Ducat

art.description: ghost of a principal lighthouse keeper in his forties, square weathered face, greying beard, ochre oilskin over a Board uniform with brass buttons, peaked cap with brass badge, hands clasped behind his back, streaming seawater, drained of colour, seen from the front
idle: standing upright, hands behind back, water dripping from his oilskin
head turned slightly toward the window, water dripping
chin lifted, steady stare, water running from his cap brim

dialogue: You'll be from the Hesperus. Good. You've come in time for lighting-up, miss.
The lamp was trimmed and filled by noon. Wick cut level, chimney cleaned, fountains to the brim. I have never left a light dark.
There was a gale on the fifteenth, and the box at the west landing was taking a beating. Ropes, crane handles, the lot.
Marshall would not have it lost. He was docked for gear there once already. So he and I put on our oilskins and went down to lash it.
MacArthur stayed in the kitchen. We'd be back before lighting-up.
We came back. We must have. The lamp is ready, you see. Only I cannot for the life of me remember the climb.
The sea at that landing was standing higher than I have ever seen it, and I have seen it high.
Here. The gate on the west side of the yard. Go down and fetch my men up. It's near dark and the light wants lighting.
afterwards: The west gate, miss. Fetch my men up.
It's near dark. I'll not strike the lamp short-handed.

examine: The iron railings around the crane are an inch thick.
They are folded flat like wire and wrenched out of their sockets in the rock.
A keeper's sou'wester is snagged on one bent bar, still dripping.
Water did this. It came up from below as hard as a falling building.

props.name: smashed wooden gear box wedged in a dark rock crevice, planks burst outward
examine: A box wedged into a crevice in the cliff, a hundred and ten feet above the water.
It has been smashed open. The planks are split and bent outward.
The crane handles and mooring ropes have been thrown out of it and down the rock.
This is the box Marshall would not lose twice. The sea reached it anyway.

Something lifted it, carried it and put it down.

Look up. At the very top of the cliff, two hundred feet above the sea, the turf has been peeled away in a long brown strip.
On the afternoon of the 15th the sea climbed the whole cleft.

characters.name: Donald MacArthur

art.description: ghost of a broad-shouldered Lewis man of about forty in soaked shirtsleeves, waistcoat and braces, no coat, dark hair plastered flat, drained of colour and dripping
idle: gripping a bent iron rail with both hands, looking down
head lifting to look up over his shoulder

dialogue: You came down. Good. Someone had to come down.
I was at the kitchen window. Mr Ducat and Tom were down here at the box, lashing it in the gale.
Then the sea stood up in the geo. A grey wall, taller than the crane, taller than the rail.
I didn't stop for my coat. There wasn't time for a coat. I ran out in my shirt, shouting their names.
I got to the rail. I got to them. And then it came over all three of us together.
In daylight, miss. With the lamp trimmed and ready. We were only ever going to be ten minutes.
Look up, now. Look up at the tower.
(Above the cliff the great beam swings on for the first time in eleven nights. MacArthur lifts his face to it, and he is gone.)
afterwards: (Only the bent rail, wet where his hands were. Far above, the beam goes round and round.)

dialogue: Three came down to lash the line.
Three I took, and three are mine.
Will you come down and count them?
